loopAccuracy of 3 Dimensional Transoesophageal Echocardiography in Assessment of Prosthetic MitralThe supplementary movies demonstrate the prosthetic mitral valve paravalvular dehiscence and severe regurgitation using Apical 2 chamber 2-Dimensional Transthoracic Echocardiography (Online Video 1) and in more detail using mid-oesophageal 2-Dimensional Transoesophageal Echocardiography with colour Doppler (Online Videos 2 and 3). The sutures can be clearly seen on the atrial surface of the prosthetic mitral valve. Real-time 3-Dimensional Transoesophageal Echocardiography accurately shows the crescent shaped postero-medial paravalvular dehiscence from the atrial aspect (Online Video 4) compared to ventricular aspect (Online Video 5). Another a movie clip, three years later, a smaller mass compared to Figure 1Wikimedia CommonsStudy →▶ Cine loopEcho · Cine loopNormal and shear strains of the left ventricle in healthy human subjects measured by twoAnimation illustrating the myocardial sheets motion proposed by LeGrice et al. 2 . On the cross-section of LV, myocardial sheets with the width of 4 myocytes separated by cleavage planes of loose connective tissue could be identified. When myocardial cells contract, the myocardial sheets slide on each other causing shear strain. The myocardial sheets approached the LV endocardium obliquely from the apical direction, becoming nearly parallel to the endocardial surface in LVPW while, in the IVS, the sheets approached the LV endocardium rather vertically from the opposite direction. This difference in sheets orientation at end-diastole would cause difference in systolic radial strain between IVS and LVPW. Myocardial sheets slide relative to each other and change orientation from end diastole to end systole, and this sliding (shearing) motion pushes the endocardium towards the LV cavity, which is more prominent in LVPW than IVS. As a result, both radial normal strain and shear strain are significantly larger in LVPW than in IVS.Wikimedia CommonsStudy →▶ Cine loopEcho · Cine loopPreoperative scallop by scallop assessment of mitral prolapse using 2D transthoracic2D-TTE parasternal long-axis view: mitral valve prolapse involving A2 segment and P2 scallop. Transoesophageal long-axis view of the aortic valve. Visualization of a long vegetation (A) (larger axis: 26 mm) on the atrial side of the mitral valve, with insertion on the aortic ring (B) and reduced. It was still possible to visualize the morphological distortion of the aortic cusps, its eccentric closure (bicuspid) as well as a filamentar image in the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) (C), probably in concordance with other vegetation (C). There was a large aortic regurgitation jet, anteriorly directed to the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. In relation with mitral valve involvement by the vegetation, but equally as possible injury of the aortic jet, there was a perforation of the anterior leaflet with an important regurgitation jet. ECG recording was notable for a large atrio-ventricular conduction delay.Wikimedia CommonsStudy →▶ Cine loopEcho · Cine loopUncommon acquired Gerbode defect following extensive bicuspid aortic valve endocarditisClip S5 and Clip S6. Around the perimeter of the scan, several coronary vessels can be seen.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0153 · short axis valveThe short axis image shown here exemplifies the mitral valve annulus and it's proximity to the aortic valve. This particular specimen also exhibits a large coronary sinus ostium, seen to the left of the right atrium.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0148 · short axis valveThis short-axis scan section shows three of the four valves within the heart. Both the anterior and posterior and anterior leaflets of the mitral valve can be seen within the center of the thick-walled left ventricle. All three leaflets of the tricuspid valve can also be seen (septal running along the border between the right and left ventricles at the mid-section of the scan, anterior, then posterior moving clockwise around the center of the ventricle). The three leaflets of the pulmonary valves can also be seen at the top of the scan.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0145 · short axis valveThis MR slice of the heart clearly shows the junction of the cardiac skeleton between the aortic, mitral and tricuspid valves.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0143 · short axis valvePart of the non coronary cusp of the aortic valve (in the center of the image) can be seen in this short axis slice of the heart. This specimen also exhibits a significant amount of epicardial fat on the right side of the heart, to the right of the image.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0142 · short axis valveThe short axis slice of the heart can be used to compare the four annuli of the cardiac valves. In this specimen we can also see the right coronary artery wrap around the back of the right atrium.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0141 · short axis valveThis MR slice of the heart clearly shows the junction of the cardiac skeleton between the aortic, mitral and tricuspid valves.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0140 · short axis valveThe tri leaflet structure of the aortic valve can be seen in the center of this short axis slice of the heart at the valve level. The annulus of the mitral valve is also clearly identifiable.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0139 · short axis valveThis short axis slice of the heart nicely shows two of the coronary vessels: the right coronary artery branching off the aorta (to the right of the image) and the coronary sinus wrapping around the back of the mitral annulus (to the left of the image).University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0188 · short axis ventricleThis short axis scan section shows a mid-ventricular representation of the heart. The thick left ventricular wall and inter-ventricular septum surround the anterior and posterior papillary muscles within the chamber. The right ventricular anterior and posterior papillary muscles can also be seen. This scan provides an excellent contrast of the difference in left and right ventricular thickness and shape.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0170 · short axis ventricleThis short axis scan section shows a mid-ventricular representation of the heart. The thick left ventricular wall and inter-ventricular septum surround the anterior and posterior papillary muscles within the chamber. The right ventricular anterior and posterior papillary muscles can also be seen. This scan provides an excellent contrast of the difference in left and right ventricular thickness and shape.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0153 · short axis ventricleSignificant hypertrophy of the left ventricle can be seen in this short axis slice of the heart. Such an increase in the ventricular wall thickness results in the enlargement of the papillary complexes and the stiffening of the ventricular walls.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0148 · short axis ventricleThis short axis scan section shows a mid-ventricular representation of the heart. The thick left ventricular wall and inter-ventricular septum surround the anterior and posterior papillary muscles within the chamber. The right ventricular anterior and posterior papillary muscles can also be seen. Near the bottom of the scan, the left anterior descending coronary artery can be seen as it runs down the septum.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0145 · short axis ventricleThe differences in the papillary muscles of the left and right ventricles are clearly defined in this short axis MR slice.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0143 · short axis ventricleThe cross sectional view of the left and right ventricles, as displayed in this short axis MR slice, highlights the differences between the left and the right sides of the heart.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0142 · short axis ventricleThe papillary muscles of the left ventricle are clearly defined in this short axis MR slice through the ventricles.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0141 · short axis ventricleThis specimen show the signs of some ventricular dilation possibly due to cardiomyopathy or congestive heart failure. The intricate trabeculation of the left and right ventricles can be clearly seen in the image.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0140 · short axis ventricleThis short axis slice from a heart with no medically recorded cardiac pathologies shows some slight dilation to the chambers. This is most probably due to the age of the patient and shows how a heart can exhibit some of the anatomical symptoms of the early stages of cardiac disease without effecting the global organ function. Interestingly, this heart shows a relatively large epicardial fat pad on the anterior surface of the heart (to the top of the image).University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0139 · short axis ventricleThis short axis slice of the ventricles shows the significant hypertrophy of the left ventricle and the dilation of the right. It can be seen that the wall thickness of the left side is comparable to the chamber diameter, this ratio results in a very strong ventricle moving a small volume of blood, usually against a large ventricular afterload. The patient was diagnosed with chronic pulmonary obstruction and hypertension which over time have caused the dilation of the right ventricle and the hypertrophy of the left.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0188 · 4 chamberThis four chamber slice nicely illustrates the anterior and posterior papillary muscles of the left atrium interacting with the mitral valve. The chordae tendinae can be seen extending from the papillary muscles to the valve in both the right and left ventricles. The scan shows the contrast in wall thickness between the left and right ventricles.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0170 · 4 chamberThis four chamber slice nicely illustrates the anterior and posterior papillary muscles of the left atrium interacting with the mitral valve. The chordae tendinae can be seen extending from the papillary muscles to the valve in both the right and left ventricles. The scan shows the contrast in wall thickness between the left and right ventricles.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0153 · 4 chamberThe hypertrophy of the left ventricle can be seen in this four chamber long axis view as evidenced by the thick walls of the free wall and the septum. Slight dilation of the left atrium can also be seen in the image.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0148 · 4 chamberThis four chamber slice contrasts the thickness and shape of the left and right ventricles. The tricuspid and mitral valves can be seen separating the atria from the ventricles. Note the papillary muscles and corresponding chordae tendinae.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0145 · 4 chamberThe left and the right chambers of the heart as well as the left ventricular outflow tract and the start of the aorta are clearly visible in this long axis image.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0143 · 4 chamberThe four chamber view of the heart shows the differences between the left and the right sides of the heart as well as the significant amounts of epicardial fat on the right side, to the right of the image. Interestingly, the image also indicates that this heart has a atrial septal defect, a hole between the right and left atrium.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0142 · 4 chamberAlthough not clinically diagnosed the anatomical structure of this large heart indicates the progression of a dilated cardiomyopathy. This diagnosis is based upon the ratio of the ventricular wall thickness and the chamber volumes.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0141 · 4 chamberThe four chamber view of this heart shows evidence of ventricular dilation, thin ventricular wall and large chamber volumes.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0140 · 4 chamberThis four chamber slice of the heart exhibits the dilation of the left atrium. Additionally, the image beautifully shows one of the papillary heads of a complex in the left ventricle, note that the head of the papillary muscle has two distinctive tips that connect to both the anterior and posterior leaflets of the mitral valve.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0139 · 4 chamberThe very thick walls and small volume of the left ventricle can be seen in this four chamber view of the heart. In contrast the right ventricle and atrium show signs of dilation caused by chronic pulmonary obstruction.University of Minnesota Cardiac AtlasStudy →Cardiac MRI · Still imageHeart0188 · 2 chamber leftThis two chamber slice exhibits the left side of the heart. This scan shows the anterior papillary muscle attaching to the mitral valve via the chordae tendinae. Note the proximity of the aortic and mitral valves.
